extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of periodical essays interested in manners, morals, art criticism, and domestic conduct (early-18th-century literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Short essays or letters that instruct or critique social behaviour, virtue, and the arts—aimed at persuading a broad literate audience about taste, morals, and domestic conduct. Emphasises examples, anecdotes, and prescriptive commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wise picture (criteria for a good painting)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'wise Picture' is one that is 'thoroughly understood in the Whole, and well performed in the Particulars' — begun on the foundation of geometry, carried on by the rules of perspective, architecture, and anatomy, and perfected by a good harmony, a just and natural colouring, and such passions and expressions of the mind as are almost peculiar to Raphael.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast a 'wise' picture (well-studied, grounded in principles and knowledge of nature) with a merely 'witty' picture that only affects the eye; a good painting should represent a well-chosen part of Nature, incorporate learned principles (geometry/perspective/anatomy), harmonious composition, natural colouring, and expressive passions. Avoid works that are only showy or gaudy for their own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gaudy show over true imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures (and by analogy persons and speeches) that only please the eye with a show of colours or loudness are inferior to those that truly imitate nature and are well-considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be misled by surface splendour: a flashy display (gaudy colouring, loud speaking, ostentatious dress) can be mistaken for merit by the hasty; cultivate judgment by study and observation of nature to distinguish genuine excellence from mere show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositional lighting and focal clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be but one forcible light in a Picture which should catch the Eye and fall on the Hero; as the Shadows represent melancholy and the Lights the bright and lively Thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a single dominant light/source to focus attention and clarify the principal subject; arrange lights and shadows so they correspond to mood and narrative emphasis. Metaphorically: in writing/images, have a clear focal idea/object of affection rather than diffuse attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reasoned observation to judge art
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Man when he looks on a Picture should examine it according to that share of Reason he is Master of, or he will be in danger of making a wrong Judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate habit of observing nature and learning relevant principles so judgments are not hasty; deliberate inspection prevents mistaking boldness or impudence for true greatness. Applies to readers and critics as well as creators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict virtue as amiable and attractive
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is in itself of an amiable nature and an ornament to human nature; it should be represented as lovely — not only as duty but as a source of happiness and admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying virtuous characters, emphasise qualities that incline them to do good to mankind (justice, charity, munificence) and traits that make virtue socially attractive (cheerfulness and good-nature). Avoid reducing virtue to mere austerity or pedantry — show its social, humane, and pleasing effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight those virtues that make characters beloved
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular virtues are more beloved because they render us beneficial to one another: Justice, Charity, Munificence, and similar qualities that dispose us to do good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In storytelling or character sketches, foreground actions and traits that produce tangible benefit to others; these will generally evoke more affection from readers than abstruse moralizing (temperance/devotion may be laudable but less immediately popular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent virtue from becoming severity or censoriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheerfulness and Good-Nature are the two great ornaments of Virtue; they keep out melancholy and prevent hatred of vice from souring into severity and censoriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid portraying virtuous people as sour, censorious martyrs; balance moral seriousness with warmth and good humour to make them sympathetic and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for making absence in love bearable (dramatic/epistolary devices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical consolations for absent lovers include agreed daily hours to think of one another, shared prayers at a set hour, ritualised visits to each other's pictures/places, and even imaginative inventions for instant correspondence (the anecdotal 'sympathetic needle' dial-plate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rituals, shared habits, and symbolic devices in fiction/letters to make separation feel plausible and emotionally convincing. Small repeated actions (appointed hours, prayers, token objects) dramatise connection across distance and can be used as narrative motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of moving domestic distress ('beautiful distress')
rubrics_metrics.description: A moving scene (called 'Beautiful Distress') arises from believable, low-life incidents: a frugal wife's secret saving, a husband's betrayal by selling a lottery ticket, the wife's subsequent fainting and madness—real circumstances producing sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In writing pathos, ground emotion in ordinary, concrete details and credible consequences; avoid contrivance and allow the natural injustice and human frailty of the situation to evoke pity rather than relying on melodramatic exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproach licentious public speech and protect modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Licentious, indecent language uttered in public (stage-boxes, assemblies, pews) inflicts deep suffering upon modest persons and therefore merits repeated invective and, where necessary, prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing social scenes, show how rude or indecent speech harms bystanders—use moral censure and, if appropriate, appeal to public regulation (e.g., the royal injunction forbidding admission behind the scenes) to defend public decency. This is both a social and narrative criterion for plausibility and moral stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer innocent, domestic pastimes to disreputable gambling
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend winter evening diversions that are merry and innocent (Hot-Cockles, Questions and Commands, Mottoes, Similes, Cross-Purposes, Blind-Man's Buff) instead of gambling games like Whisk, Lanterloo, or One and Thirty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In scenes of domestic recreation, choose activities that produce good-humoured sociability and are appropriate to family life; these choices signal character and reinforce moral tone. Describe the games' physicality and comic mishaps to produce amusement without moral compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing abstruse philosophical pedantry in domestic settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic peace is disturbed when young people impose abstruse speculations (e.g., denying the reality of pleasure and pain, disputing obvious colours) on elders; such pedantry can be intolerable and disruptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterise learned or pedantic figures carefully: show the social friction their abstract talk causes, especially in contexts where quiet and common sense are expected. Use the contrast for comic or critical effect, but beware of making pedagogy itself the point rather than its social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure ingratitude and ridicule of honest plainness
rubrics_metrics.description: A species of people who are ugly and ill-natured (the 'Apes') take delight in ridiculing the plainness and sincerity of others—this ingratitude and malicious mockery is itself a deep vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting social satire, mark the cruelty of nickname-calling and cheap wit; show its corrosive social effects and differentiate genuine wit from spiteful ridicule. Use such examples to teach readers to beware of malicious amusement and to prefer charitable judgment.
